meta.title: African Engineering, Organized for Sustainable Growth | MRVIN100
meta.description: An open, country-adapted framework for organizing African engineering talent, supporting fair work, stronger delivery, mentorship and local capability.

hero.badge: A framework for African engineering capacity
hero.subtitle: MRVIN100 is building a country-adapted framework that helps organizations work with African engineers, grow capability locally and make the economics clear.

evidence.title: A clear source behind every figure.
evidence.description: The overview keeps direct digital-sector value separate from value enabled in other sectors. Every figure includes its year, scope, source and limitations.

items.title: Mobile technologies and services
items.text: GSMA estimates the mobile ecosystem’s contribution to Africa’s economy. This is broad digital-economy context, not software-engineering revenue.

items.title: Online job postings analysed
items.text: A World Bank study examined postings from Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa and Uganda. Online postings overrepresent formal, higher-skilled roles and do not equal software vacancies.
items.source: World Bank · Digital Skills for Africa

items.title: Jobs supported by the mobile ecosystem
items.text: The GSMA estimates the mobile ecosystem supported about 13 million jobs across Africa in 2025. This is a broad digital-economy indicator, not a developer headcount.

evidence.distinctionTitle: Two kinds of value. Two separate measures.
evidence.directText: Revenue and value added from software, digital services and technology businesses.
evidence.enabledText: Measured changes in cost, productivity, access or service quality when organizations use digital systems.
evidence.methodNote: We will not turn a mobile-economy estimate or a single project result into a continent-wide software-market figure.

framework.title: Shared principles. Country-specific practice.
framework.description: The framework sets clear commitments and allows local maintainers to adapt implementation to laws, currencies, labor markets and operating realities.

principles.title: Fair, local compensation
principles.text: Aim for compensation in the upper 30% of comparable country-specific salary ranges, using recent local evidence and publishing the method.

principles.title: Capability grows through work
principles.text: Pair real delivery with structured mentorship from experienced engineers to early-career talent.

principles.title: Transparent economics
principles.text: Show how pricing supports engineer compensation, delivery, mentorship and sustainable operations.

principles.title: Quality and accountability
principles.text: Set clear expectations for scope, communication, delivery, feedback and how problems are resolved.

principles.title: Local adaptation, open governance
principles.text: Keep a shared core, publish country addenda, record changes and invite feedback from practitioners.

framework.statusNote: The upper-30% pay position is a target to validate country by country, not a published salary guarantee. Rules and benchmarks require dated local sources.

adoption.title: A framework others can shape and use.
adoption.description: Companies, agencies, public institutions and developer networks can explore the framework and help adapt it. Adoption is voluntary; using the MRVIN100 name should require a clear, published commitment.

useCasesPage.title: Use cases
useCasesPage.subtitle: MRVIN100 is intended to help different actors organize engineering work and grow local capability. These are intended contributions, not measured outcomes or guarantees.

items.q: Is MRVIN100 a company or a model?
items.a: MRVIN100 is an open framework for organizing African engineering talent. Organizations and practitioners can adopt and help develop it. The framework is not a software platform or a two-sided hiring marketplace.

items.q: Does MRVIN100 prescribe one fixed developer share?
items.a: No fixed percentage has been adopted. The model calls for transparent project economics and locally evidenced compensation. Its stated pay direction is to target the upper 30% of comparable salaries by country, role and experience; that target still needs a published method and current evidence.

items.q: Does the model guarantee lower prices than offshore providers?
items.a: No. MRVIN100 asks organizations to compare scope, total cost, local context, accountability and quality. Prices depend on the work, country, experience and contract. The framework aims to make assumptions visible, not promise a discount.

items.q: Does every project need a delivery manager?
items.a: No. Each engagement should name who owns planning, technical decisions, review, communication, acceptance and handover. A delivery coordinator may help when the work needs one, but MRVIN100 does not currently mandate a specific role or project cap.
No shared replacement window has been adopted. Any availability, replacement or remedy commitment must be agreed in the project contract and checked against local law.
No. The atlas maps countries, but a mapped boundary does not mean validated market data or local adoption. Each profile should publish dated sources and clearly show missing evidence.
